title: Hands-on Exercise 2
section: 14.1 Testing Against a Null That Is Not a Strawman
text:
14.1 Testing Against a Null That Is Not a Strawman
Everything so far compares childcare centres to a pattern where any point in Singapore is equally likely, including reservoirs, the airport, industrial estates and military land. At least Jurong Island was dropped with the offshore subzones at the start.
Floch et al. raise this for French pharmacies, where regulation ties locations to population. They say CSR “does not appear to be the most relevant” reference there. Childcare centres similarly follow housing. So the clustering result may only tell me that Singapore’s residents are clustered, which I already knew.
The reading suggests a fix. Kinhom() drops the assumption of constant intensity and compares the pattern against a null that uses the observed intensity. If the centres still clump beyond that, the clustering is real. If not, it was caused by population.
density() with bw.diggle estimates the intensity surface for Choa Chu Kang, and range() checks its values.

lambda_ck <- density(childcare_ck_ppp, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE)
range(lambda_ck$v, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 5.030384e-10 4.086766e-05








NoteLearning diary



My surface is entirely positive, but I clamp it anyway.
The book’s own output in section 4.7.1 has a density range starting at -6.58e-21. That is floating point noise from the edge correction, not a real negative density, and it does not show on the plot.
It only matters when the surface goes to rpoispp() for the simulation below, which refuses a negative intensity with a “negative probability” error that does not say where the negative came from. Whether you hit it depends on your data.
Adding one line now is easier than debugging that later.


The clamp sets any negative cell to zero, then counts how many there were.

lambda_pos <- lambda_ck
lambda_pos$v[lambda_pos$v < 0] <- 0

# confirm whether the clamp actually had anything to do
sum(lambda_ck$v < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 0


Kinhom() of spatstat computes the inhomogeneous K with that surface as lambda, plotted against pi d^2 the same way as K above.

The PlotThe Code














par(cex.main = 1.3, cex.sub = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.1, mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))
Kinhom_ck <- Kinhom(childcare_ck_ppp, lambda = lambda_pos,
                    correction = "Ripley")
plot(Kinhom_ck, (. - pi * r^2) / 1e6 ~ r,
     ylab = "Kinhom(d) - pi d^2 (km sq)", xlab = "d (m)",
     col = c("black", "#D55E00"),
     main = "Inhomogeneous K, intensity taken from the data")




With the intensity taken from the data, the curve falls below zero and keeps falling, to about -0.7 km sq by 800 m. Taken literally, this means the centres have fewer neighbours than the local intensity predicts.
envelope() with Kinhom and simulate = expression(rpoispp(lambda_pos)) draws 39 patterns from the estimated intensity instead of from CSR. Black is observed, orange dashed is the mean of the simulated patterns and grey is their pointwise range. The legend is off so it cannot cover the band.

The PlotThe Code














par(cex.main = 1.3, cex.sub = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.1, mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))
Kinhom_ck.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kinhom,
                          simulate = expression(rpoispp(lambda_pos)),
                          nsim = 39, verbose = FALSE)
plot(Kinhom_ck.csr, (. - pi * r^2) / 1e6 ~ r, xlab = "d (m)",
     ylab = "Kinhom(d) - pi d^2 (km sq)", legend = FALSE,
     col = c("black", "#D55E00", "grey", "grey"),
     main = "Inhomogeneous K against a population-shaped null")




Here the observed curve stays close to zero and inside the band at every distance. Once the local intensity is accounted for, Choa Chu Kang shows no extra clustering.






ImportantCheck that caught something



The black curve here ends near -0.05 km sq, but the previous plot of the same data ended near -0.7. They are different estimates. In the earlier plot I passed lambda_pos, built from these same points with a narrow bw.diggle bandwidth. So each centre’s intensity includes its own kernel and comes out too high, which pulls K down. Inside envelope() I did not pass lambda, so Kinhom() estimated it itself and left each point out of its own intensity. That leave-one-out estimate is the one to trust, so the deep dip earlier is mostly an artefact.








TipAlternative explored



This uses the same K function for a different question. Kest asks whether centres are more clustered than a uniform scatter. Kinhom asks whether they are more clustered than the local intensity already implies.
Compare this plot with the Kest one further up. Any gap left here is clustering that population density does not explain.
One caveat is that the null comes from the same data it is tested against, so it is not independent evidence. Floch et al. warn that bias appears when the smoothing window is close in size to the r values being tested.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
14.2 Cumulative Against Density
K counts every neighbour out to r, so it is cumulative. A bump at 400 metres could come from tight clustering at 50 metres still carried in the total.
The pair correlation function counts in a ring at distance r instead of a disc out to r. So it shows the distance where clustering happens, not where it has built up.
pcf() of spatstat estimates it. It shoots up near zero distance, so I cap the y axis at 4 to keep the rest readable.

The PlotThe Code














par(cex.main = 1.3, cex.sub = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.1, mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))
pcf_ck <- pcf(childcare_ck_ppp)
plot(pcf_ck, main = "Pair correlation, Choa Chu Kang",
     xlab = "d (m)", ylim = c(0, 4), legendpos = "topright",
     col = c("black", "#0072B2", "#D55E00"))
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "#D55E00")










TipAlternative explored



Under randomness the pair correlation is 1, shown by the dashed line. Above 1 means more neighbours at that exact distance than chance would give.
Its advantage over K is that it pins down the distance of the clustering. Its disadvantage is that only a cumulative function can detect clusters of clusters. They answer different questions, so one does not replace the other.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
section: 14.3 Redoing G With a Global Envelope
text:
14.3 Redoing G With a Global Envelope
The earlier G test used a pointwise envelope, which inflates the false positive rate across the r values tested. Here I rerun it with envelope() set to global = TRUE and rank = 1 over 39 simulations.

The PlotThe Code














par(cex.main = 1.3, cex.sub = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.1, mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2))
G_ck.global <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Gest, nsim = 39, rank = 1,
                        global = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
plot(G_ck.global, xlab = "d (m)", ylim = c(0, 1),
     col = c("black", "#D55E00", "grey", "grey"),
     main = "G with a global envelope, Choa Chu Kang")




The curve stays inside the global band at every distance, including the short-distance jump that left the pointwise band. The band’s upper edge at zero distance is already about 0.27, above the 0.19 jump.






TipAlternative explored



The correction makes a global band wider than a pointwise one, so it is harder to reject the null, as intended.
If the curve still leaves the band, the result survives the multiple testing problem. If not, the original finding was partly an artefact of testing at every r and reporting the crossings.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
14.4 A Second Opinion on Randomness
All the tests so far are distance based. A quadrat test, from the other family, divides the region into cells and compares the counts against a Poisson expectation. quadrat.test() of spatstat runs it on a 4 by 4 grid.

quadrat_ck <- quadrat.test(childcare_ck_ppp, nx = 4, ny = 4)
quadrat_ck


    Chi-squared test of CSR using quadrat counts

data:  childcare_ck_ppp
X2 = 21.603, df = 12, p-value = 0.08444
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Quadrats: 13 tiles (irregular windows)








WarningIssue I hit



I first stored this as qt, which is base R’s t-distribution quantile function. R refused with “cannot change value of locked binding”.
It is the same mistake as naming something c or df, so I should check a name is free first.








ImportantCheck that caught something



The quadrat test does not agree with Clark-Evans.
Clark-Evans gave R of 0.84 with p of 0.0089, rejecting randomness for Choa Chu Kang. The quadrat test on the same points gives p of 0.084, so it does not. On one dataset, the two tests reach opposite conclusions at the five percent level.
Neither is wrong, because they measure different things. Clark-Evans looks at nearest neighbour distances, so it notices points in tight pairs. The quadrat test only counts points per cell, so a pattern can be clumpy inside cells and still even across them.
The tile count also changed. I asked for a four by four grid, which is sixteen cells, but the output says thirteen tiles and twelve degrees of freedom. Three cells fell outside the planning area boundary and were dropped, and twelve is thirteen minus one. So the tested grid is not the one I specified.








TipAlternative explored



The quadrat result depends entirely on the grid I picked. A different nx and ny would change it.
This is the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem again, which I met in Exercise 1 when aggregating subzones to planning areas. The reading gives it as one of the main reasons to prefer distance-based methods.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
4.1 Counts Against Rates
geom_histogram() and geom_boxplot() of ggplot2 compare the radio count with the radio rate. ggarrange() of ggpubr puts the four charts in one figure.

The PlotThe Code














eda_hist <- function(var, title) {
  ggplot(ict_derived, aes(x = .data[[var]])) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#56B4E9", colour = "white") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Townships", title = title) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))
}

eda_box <- function(var) {
  ggplot(ict_derived, aes(x = .data[[var]])) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "#56B4E9", outlier.colour = "#D55E00",
                 outlier.size = 2.5) +
    labs(x = var, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
}

ggarrange(eda_hist("RADIO", "Radio count"),
          eda_hist("RADIO_PR", "Radio per 1,000 households"),
          eda_box("RADIO"), eda_box("RADIO_PR"),
          ncol = 2, nrow = 2, heights = c(2, 1))




The radio count is strongly right skewed. Its three outliers, Taunggyi, Lashio and Nyaungshwe, are the three townships with the most households. Taunggyi alone has 30,176 radios. The rate is much closer to symmetric, with 1 high outlier left. The top rate is in Ywangan, a small township, and not Taunggyi.

4.2 Distribution of All Six Rates
The book builds six histograms and joins them with ggarrange(). I use pivot_longer() and facet_wrap() instead, which gives the same six panels from one call.

  facet_wrap(~ variable, ncol = 3, scales = "free_x") +

                     select(ict_derived, -DT_PCODE, -DT, -TS),
                     by = "TS_PCODE")







CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book joins the full table, so the district and township columns appear twice. R renames them TS.x and TS.y, and the rest of the chapter has to use TS.x. All 55 codes match and the names agree in every case, so I drop the duplicate columns from the csv before joining. The township column stays TS. The book also saves and reloads the joined data as an rds file. I skip that because freeze: true already stops the page from re-running.

text:
4.4 Choropleth Maps
tm_shape() and tm_polygons() of tmap map the number of households, the radio count and the radio rate. Each uses Jenks natural breaks with five classes, as in the book. tmap_arrange() puts them side by side.

Households and radio countHouseholds and radio rateThe Code

























jenks_map <- function(var, legend_title, title) {
  tm_shape(shan_sf) +
    tm_polygons(fill = var,
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5,
                                                values = "brewer.blues"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = legend_title,
                                        position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
                col = "grey60") +
    tm_title(title, size = 1.3, fontface = "bold")
}

tmap_arrange(jenks_map("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "Households", "Total households"),
             jenks_map("RADIO", "Radios", "Radio count"),
             ncol = 2)

tmap_arrange(jenks_map("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "Households", "Total households"),
             jenks_map("RADIO_PR", "Per 1,000", "Radio per 1,000 households"),
             ncol = 2)




The household map and the radio count map look almost the same. Both are dark around Taunggyi and Lashio. The rate map is different. Its highest classes run down the west side of the state, while much of the north east is pale. This confirms the rates and not the counts should go into the clustering.






CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book uses tmap v3 code such as tm_fill(style = "jenks"), tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) and qtm(). These give deprecation messages in tmap 4.4, so I rewrote every map in v4 syntax with fill.scale, fill.legend and tm_title(). All legends sit outside the map.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.4 Computing the Proximity Matrix
dist() computes the Euclidean distance between every pair of townships across the five rates.

proxmat <- dist(shan_ict, method = "euclidean")







CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book shows both scaling methods and then builds the distance matrix from the raw rates in shan_ict. I do the same in the main part so my results can be checked against the book. But it has a cost. A rate with a wide range adds more to the distance. In the section Raw Rates Against Z-scores I measure how much and rerun the clustering on z-scores.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.5 Selecting the Clustering Algorithm
agnes() of cluster reports an agglomerative coefficient for each linkage method. Values closer to 1 mean a stronger cluster structure. map_dbl() of purrr runs it for four methods.

m <- c("average", "single", "complete", "ward")
names(m) <- c("average", "single", "complete", "ward")

ac <- function(x) {
  agnes(shan_ict, method = x)$ac
}

map_dbl(m, ac)

  average    single  complete      ward 
0.8131144 0.6628705 0.8950702 0.9427730 


Ward’s method gives the highest coefficient, 0.943, so I use it from here on.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.6 Computing the Hierarchical Clustering
hclust() of base R builds the tree with Ward’s method.

hclust_ward <- hclust(proxmat, method = "ward.D2")







CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book uses method = "ward.D". R has two Ward options. ward.D2 squares the distances before merging, which is Ward’s original criterion. ward.D does not. The agnes() check above and the hcut() used for the gap statistic below both use the squared version. So ward.D2 keeps the whole section on one method. The two trees do give different results. Cut at six clusters, they only agree with an adjusted Rand index of 0.77, where 1 means identical. So my clusters will not match the book’s.

clusGap() of cluster computes the gap statistic for 1 to 10 clusters. It compares how tight the clusters are with how tight they would be in random data. hcut() of factoextra does the clustering inside it.

gap_stat <- clusGap(shan_ict,
                    FUN = hcut,
                    nstart = 25,
                    K.max = 10,
                    B = 50)
print(gap_stat, method = "firstmax")

[10,] 7.377412 7.593858 0.2164465 0.04540947


fviz_gap_stat() of factoextra plots the result.

The PlotThe Code














fviz_gap_stat(gap_stat, linecolor = "#0072B2") +
  labs(title = "The gap statistic is highest at one cluster",
       subtitle = "Among two or more clusters, six has the largest gap",
       x = "Number of clusters", y = "Gap statistic") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"))




The gap statistic recommends one cluster, which is no use for segmentation. Among two or more clusters, six has the largest gap at 0.2222. But five is at 0.2216, almost the same. Like the book, I go with six. I come back to whether six is a good choice in How Many Clusters.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.8 Interpreting the Dendrogram
plot() draws the tree and rect.hclust() boxes the six clusters.

The PlotThe Code














okabe6 <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#CC79A7", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#F0E442")

plot(hclust_ward, cex = 0.6, xlab = "", sub = "",
     main = "Ward's tree of Shan townships, cut into six clusters",
     cex.main = 1.5, las = 1)
rect.hclust(hclust_ward, k = 6, border = okabe6)










CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book draws the boxes with border = 2:5. That is four base R colours for six boxes, so two are reused, and one of them is green. I use six Okabe-Ito colours without green, which I set once as okabe6 and reuse for every cluster map below.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.9 Visually-driven Hierarchical Clustering
heatmaply() of heatmaply draws an interactive heatmap with a dendrogram of the rows. It needs a matrix, so data.matrix() converts the data frame first.

shan_ict_mat <- data.matrix(shan_ict)


The PlotThe Code











heatmaply(normalize(shan_ict_mat),
          Colv = NA,
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D2",
          seriate = "OLO",
          colors = Blues,
          k_row = 6,
          margins = c(NA, 200, 60, NA),
          fontsize_row = 4,
          fontsize_col = 5,
          main = "Geographic Segmentation of Shan State by ICT indicators",
          xlab = "ICT Indicators",
          ylab = "Townships of Shan State")










NoteLearning diary



The six row groups in the heatmap are not the same six clusters as the dendrogram above. heatmaply() clusters the data it is given, and here that is normalize(shan_ict_mat), the min-max version. The dendrogram used the raw rates. I first assumed the heatmap was just a picture of my clusters, but it is a second clustering. It is useful for seeing which rates are high or low in each group of rows. The cluster labels should come from cutree().

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.10 Mapping the Clusters
cutree() cuts the tree into six groups. I add them to shan_sf as a factor column.

groups <- as.factor(cutree(hclust_ward, k = 6))
shan_sf_cluster <- shan_sf %>%
  mutate(CLUSTER = groups)
table(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER)


 1  2  3  4  5  6 
16  8 13  6  7  5 



The PlotThe Code














cluster_map <- function(data, var, title, title_size = 1.5) {
  tm_shape(data) +
    tm_polygons(fill = var,
                fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = okabe6),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Cluster",
                                        position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
                col = "grey40") +
    tm_title(title, size = title_size, fontface = "bold")
}

cluster_map(shan_sf_cluster, "CLUSTER",
            "Hierarchical clusters are scattered across the state")




The clusters are fragmented. Most of them appear in several separate places on the map. This is expected, because hierarchical clustering only looks at the ICT rates and not at location. Two townships far apart can end up in the same cluster if their rates are similar. For a segmentation that can be used to plan by region, this is a problem. The next two methods add location.

CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book first converts shan_sf to a SpatialPolygonsDataFrame with as_Spatial(), because older versions of spdep needed sp objects. Current spdep accepts sf directly, so I skip the conversion.


st_centroid() gives each township a point, so the links can be drawn.

coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(shan_sf)))

     main = "Queen neighbours of Shan townships", cex.main = 1.5)

shan.w <- nb2listw(shan.nb, lcosts, style = "B")

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
7.3 Computing the Minimum Spanning Tree
mstree() of spdep finds the minimum spanning tree. This is the set of links that connects all townships with the lowest total cost and no loops.

set.seed(1234)
shan.mst <- mstree(shan.w)
dim(shan.mst)

[1] 54  3

head(shan.mst)

     [,1] [,2]      [,3]
[1,]   28   12  78.78999
[2,]   12   49  59.69478
[3,]   28   13  92.79567
[4,]   13   52 110.55197
[5,]   49   35 124.74445
[6,]   35   37  91.65458


The tree has 54 links for 55 townships, one fewer than the number of townships, as a tree should. Each row gives the two townships and the cost of the link.






NoteLearning diary



mstree() starts from a random township when ini is not given, so I added set.seed(). I tried a few seeds. The start point changed the order of the rows but not the cluster sizes SKATER produced, because the tree itself is the same.



The PlotThe Code














plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), border = "grey60",
     main = "Minimum spanning tree of Shan townships", cex.main = 1.5)
plot.mst(shan.mst, coords, col = "#0072B2",
         cex.lab = 0.7, cex.circles = 0.005, add = TRUE)




Compared with the neighbour map, most links are gone. Each township now connects to the rest of the state by only one path.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
7.4 Computing the SKATER Clusters
skater() of spdep cuts the tree. ncuts = 5 makes five cuts, which gives six clusters.

clust6 <- spdep::skater(edges = shan.mst[, 1:2],
                        data = shan_ict,
                        method = "euclidean",
                        ncuts = 5)
ccs6 <- clust6$groups
table(ccs6)

ccs6
 1  2  3  4  5  6 
22 18 11  2  1  1 


The clusters are very uneven. There are three large ones and three with only one or two townships.

The PlotThe Code














plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), border = "grey60",
     main = "The spanning tree after five cuts", cex.main = 1.5)
plot(clust6, coords, cex.lab = 0.7,
     groups.colors = okabe6,
     cex.circles = 0.005, add = TRUE)










CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book passes five colours, including green, for six groups. I pass okabe6, so each group has its own colour.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
7.5 Mapping the SKATER Clusters

The PlotThe Code














shan_sf_spatialcluster <- shan_sf_cluster %>%
  mutate(SP_CLUSTER = as.factor(ccs6))

cluster_map(shan_sf_spatialcluster, "SP_CLUSTER",
            "SKATER clusters are joined-up regions")




tmap_arrange() puts the two results side by side.

The PlotThe Code














tmap_arrange(cluster_map(shan_sf_cluster, "CLUSTER",
                         "Hierarchical", title_size = 1.3),
             cluster_map(shan_sf_spatialcluster, "SP_CLUSTER",
                         "SKATER", title_size = 1.3),
             ncol = 2)




The SKATER map is much easier to read. Each cluster is one region. The cluster numbers do not match between the two maps, since each method numbers its own clusters. The cost is in the cluster sizes. SKATER puts 22 townships in its largest cluster, and three clusters are tiny. A single cut that isolates one unusual township counts as a whole cluster.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
8.1 Ward-like Hierarchical Clustering with ClustGeo
hclustgeo() with only D0 gives the non-spatial version.

The PlotThe Code














nongeo_cluster <- hclustgeo(proxmat)
plot(nongeo_cluster, cex = 0.5, xlab = "", sub = "",
     main = "ClustGeo tree with alpha = 0", cex.main = 1.5, las = 1)
rect.hclust(nongeo_cluster, k = 6, border = okabe6)





ngeo_groups <- as.factor(cutree(nongeo_cluster, k = 6))
shan_sf_ngeo_cluster <- shan_sf %>%
  mutate(CLUSTER = ngeo_groups)

adjustedRandIndex(ngeo_groups, groups)

[1] 1








ImportantCheck that caught something



The book maps these clusters as a new result. I expected them to match my hclust() clusters, since ClustGeo with alpha = 0 is plain Ward clustering. The adjusted Rand index of 1 shows they are the same six groups. ClustGeo squares the distances, like ward.D2. This is also why the book’s two maps differ. The book’s hclust() used ward.D, which does not square them. So I skip the duplicate map.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
8.2 Spatially Constrained Hierarchical Clustering
st_distance() of sf computes the distance between every pair of townships. as.dist() turns it into the D1 matrix.

dist <- st_distance(shan_sf, shan_sf)
distmat <- as.dist(dist)







NoteLearning diary



st_distance() on polygons measures the gap between their boundaries, not their centres. So any two townships that touch have a distance of 0. In this matrix 132 pairs are at 0, the same as the 132 pairs of Queen neighbours. ClustGeo treats them all as equally close, whether they share a long border or one corner.


choicealpha() of ClustGeo tries alpha from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.1. For each alpha it reports two scores. Q0 is the share of ICT variation explained by the six clusters, and Q1 is the share of spatial variation explained. Raising alpha gains Q1 and loses Q0.

cr <- choicealpha(proxmat, distmat,
                  range.alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.1),
                  K = 6, graph = FALSE)


The PlotThe Code














alpha_df <- tibble(alpha = cr$range.alpha,
                   `Q0, ICT` = cr$Q[, 1],
                   `Q1, location` = cr$Q[, 2]) %>%
  pivot_longer(-alpha, names_to = "score", values_to = "value")

ggplot(alpha_df, aes(x = alpha, y = value, colour = score)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.2, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1)) +
  labs(x = "alpha", y = "Share of variation explained", colour = NULL,
       title = "Most of the spatial gain comes by alpha = 0.2",
       subtitle = "Dashed line, the alpha used below") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "top")




At alpha 0, the clusters explain 76 percent of the ICT variation but only 13 percent of the spatial variation. At alpha 0.2, Q1 jumps to 63 percent while Q0 only falls to 65 percent. After 0.2, each step gives up roughly as much Q0 as it gains in Q1. So 0.2 is a fair compromise, and it is the value the book uses.






CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book sets graph = TRUE and uses ClustGeo’s own plot. I set it to FALSE and draw Q0 and Q1 with ggplot, so the chart has a title, labelled axes and the chosen alpha marked.


hclustgeo() with both matrices and alpha = 0.2 gives the spatially constrained tree.

clustG <- hclustgeo(proxmat, distmat, alpha = 0.2)
groups_geo <- as.factor(cutree(clustG, k = 6))
shan_sf_Gcluster <- shan_sf %>%
  mutate(CLUSTER = groups_geo)
table(shan_sf_Gcluster$CLUSTER)


 1  2  3  4  5  6 
10  9  7  9 12  8 



The PlotThe Code














tmap_arrange(cluster_map(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER",
                         "ClustGeo, alpha = 0", title_size = 1.3),
             cluster_map(shan_sf_Gcluster, "CLUSTER",
                         "ClustGeo, alpha = 0.2", title_size = 1.3),
             ncol = 2)




With alpha 0.2 the clusters are much more compact than at alpha 0, and the sizes are more even, from 7 to 12 townships. But some clusters still have a few townships away from the main block. ClustGeo only pushes nearby townships together. It does not forbid a cluster from being split.

geom_boxplot() shows the radio rate in each cluster.

The PlotThe Code

  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, outlier.size = 2.5) +

9.2 Multivariate Visualisation
ggparcoord() of GGally draws a parallel coordinate plot, one line per township, split by cluster with facet_grid().

ict_cols <- c("RADIO_PR", "TV_PR", "LLPHONE_PR", "MPHONE_PR", "COMPUTER_PR")

ggparcoord(data = profile_df,
           columns = match(ict_cols, names(profile_df)),
           scale = "uniminmax",

The book uses scale = "globalminmax", which keeps one shared scale for all five rates. Computer and landline rates are so small that their boxes sit flat at the bottom. uniminmax rescales each rate on its own from 0 to 1, so differences in computer ownership show up too. I also find the column positions by name with match() instead of typing c(17:21).

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
10.1 Raw Rates Against Z-scores
The book clusters on raw rates. To see how much each rate counts, I compare their variances. The squared Euclidean distance is a sum over the five rates, so each rate’s share of the total variance is roughly its share of the distance.

tibble(variable = names(shan_ict),
       sd = sapply(shan_ict, sd),
       share_of_variance = sapply(shan_ict, var) / sum(sapply(shan_ict, var))) %>%
  arrange(desc(share_of_variance)) %>%
  kable(digits = c(0, 1, 3))

MPHONE_PR and TV_PR together make up 81 percent of the variance. COMPUTER_PR makes up less than 1 percent. So the raw clustering mostly ignores computer ownership, even though it is one of the five chosen measures.
I rerun the same Ward clustering on the z-scores, where every rate counts equally.

hclust_z <- hclust(dist(shan_ict.z), method = "ward.D2")
groups_z <- as.factor(cutree(hclust_z, k = 6))
shan_sf_zcluster <- shan_sf %>% mutate(CLUSTER = groups_z)

adjustedRandIndex(groups, groups_z)

[1] 0.317144



The PlotThe Code














tmap_arrange(cluster_map(shan_sf_cluster, "CLUSTER",
                         "Raw rates", title_size = 1.3),
             cluster_map(shan_sf_zcluster, "CLUSTER",
                         "Z-scores", title_size = 1.3),
             ncol = 2)










TipAlternative explored



The two results agree with an adjusted Rand index of only 0.32. Scaling changed the clusters a lot, not just at the edges. With z-scores, landline and computer rates count as much as TV and mobile. The six most connected townships under the raw rates were Muse, Tachileik, Laukkaing, Mongla, Namhkan and Taunggyi. Under z-scores that top group shrinks to Muse, Tachileik, Taunggyi, the three townships with the highest computer rates. Laukkaing and Namhkan move to a group with the most landlines, and Mongla joins a middle group.
Neither version is wrong. They answer different questions. The raw version groups townships mostly by TV and mobile phone use. The z-score version weighs all five measures equally. Since the book chose five measures on purpose, I think the z-score version fits the question better.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
10.2 How Many Clusters
The gap statistic picked one cluster. I check six against two other common measures for the same Ward tree. The average silhouette width shows how well each township fits its own cluster compared with the next closest, and higher is better. The elbow method shows how much within-cluster variation is left as clusters are added.

k_check <- tibble(k = 2:10) %>%
  mutate(silhouette = map_dbl(k, ~ mean(silhouette(cutree(hclust_ward, .x),
                                                   proxmat)[, 3])),
         unexplained = map_dbl(k, ~ 1 - r_squared(cutree(hclust_ward, .x))))


The PlotThe Code














k_plot <- function(y, ylab, title) {
  ggplot(k_check, aes(x = k, y = .data[[y]])) +
    geom_line(colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = k == 6), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:10) +
    labs(x = "Number of clusters", y = ylab, title = title) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))
}

ggarrange(k_plot("silhouette", "Average silhouette width",
                 "Silhouette is best at two clusters"),
          k_plot("unexplained", "Share of variation left",
                 "No clear elbow"),
          ncol = 2)










TipAlternative explored



None of the three measures points to six. The silhouette is highest at two clusters, 0.347. At six it is 0.253, the lowest of all the values I tried. The elbow curve falls smoothly with no clear bend. Six clusters still leave 24 percent of the variation unexplained.
So six is a choice for usefulness, not something the data shows. Two clusters would only split the more connected townships from the less connected ones. That is too coarse for planning, so six is reasonable. But a silhouette around 0.25 means the clusters overlap a lot, and townships near the edges could easily go either way.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
10.3 What the Spatial Constraint Costs
I put the three main results in one table. It shows how much ICT variation each one explains, how many separate pieces it makes on the map, and how close it is to the plain hclust() result.

solutions <- list(`Hierarchical (ward.D2)` = groups,
                  `SKATER` = ccs6,
                  `ClustGeo, alpha = 0.2` = groups_geo)

cost_table <- tibble(method = names(solutions),
       ict_explained = map_dbl(solutions, r_squared),
       map_pieces = map_dbl(solutions, count_pieces),
       cluster_sizes = map_chr(solutions,
                               ~ paste(sort(table(.x), decreasing = TRUE),
                                       collapse = ", ")),
       ari_vs_hierarchical = map_dbl(solutions,
                                     ~ adjustedRandIndex(.x, groups)))
kable(cost_table, digits = 2)

TipAlternative explored



The table shows the trade-off in numbers. Hierarchical clustering explains the most ICT variation, 76 percent, but its six clusters break into 28 separate pieces on the map. SKATER gives exactly 6 pieces, one per cluster, but explains only 50 percent, and it has single-township clusters. ClustGeo sits in between, with 65 percent explained and 18 pieces.
I expected ClustGeo at alpha 0.2 to look much like SKATER, because the map was so much tidier than at alpha 0. But 18 pieces is still a lot of fragments. Most of them come from clusters 3 and 4, the least and the most connected townships. Extreme townships have no similar neighbours, so ClustGeo leaves them where their rates fit. Both spatial methods are also far from the hierarchical result, with adjusted Rand indexes of 0.18 and 0.26. So the choice of method changes the answer more than any setting within a method.
For planning by region I would use SKATER, because the clusters have to be single areas. I would merge its tiny clusters into their neighbours. ClustGeo is better when a few separate townships are acceptable and the clusters need to stay similar inside.

Hi, I am ZeXin. This site is where I keep my coursework for ISSS626 Geospatial Analytics and Applications at SMU.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Forest and land fires, Pulang Pisau regency, Central Kalimantan, 1 Jul to 22 Sep 2026 NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS, GADM 4.1, OpenStreetMap pacman sf spatstat sparr terra tmap tidyverse knitr
In short. Very little burned until late August. Fire-days then rose to a peak in the last week of the record, with the densest burning in the south-central peat. Fires that were close in space were also close in time. Fires under 3 km apart happened 1 to 3 days apart more often than random dates give, and a daily patrol zone built on this found more new fires than a hotspot map of the same size.
The task is set out in the Take-home Exercise 1 brief. The Executive Summary is here.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Data Acquisition









Dataset
Source and access
Coverage used
Notes




MODIS Collection 6.1 active fires
NASA FIRMS area API, accessed 23 Sep 2026
Kalimantan bounding box, 1 Jan to 22 Sep 2026
1 km pixels, Terra and Aqua. Standard processing to 30 Jun, near real time after


VIIRS S-NPP 375 m active fires
NASA FIRMS area API, accessed 23 Sep 2026
Same
375 m pixels (Schroeder et al., 2014). No detections at all from 28 April to 2 June or from 11 to 16 July, so used only as a sensitivity check


GADM 4.1 level 2 boundaries
gadm.org, downloaded 10 Sep 2026 for Hands-on Exercise 3
Indonesia, regency level
Used in place of the Indonesia Geospasial portal file, which failed to download


OpenStreetMap
Geofabrik Kalimantan extract, accessed 23 Sep 2026
Waterways and roads
Used for the bonus analysis (Q5)



The FIRMS data was downloaded with a short Python script through the FIRMS area API, five days at a time, for a box covering Kalimantan. It uses standard processing (SP) data up to 30 June and near real time (NRT) data after that.
To run it again, use python3 get_firms.py YOUR_MAP_KEY in data/rawdata/firms/ with a free FIRMS map key. It was run on 23 September 2026.


Show the download script, get_firms.py

"""Download FIRMS 2026 fire detections for Kalimantan through the FIRMS area API.

Usage   python3 get_firms.py YOUR_MAP_KEY
Uses standard processing (SP) data where it exists and near real time (NRT) after that.
Writes one csv per sensor into the folder this script sits in.
"""
import csv, io, sys, time, pathlib, urllib.request, datetime as dt

KEY = sys.argv[1]
OUT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent
BBOX = "108.5,-4.3,119.3,4.5"          # west,south,east,north, all of Kalimantan
START = dt.date(2026, 1, 1)
END = dt.date.today() - dt.timedelta(days=1)
BASE = "https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/api"
SENSORS = {"viirs_snpp": ("VIIRS_SNPP_SP", "VIIRS_SNPP_NRT"),
           "modis": ("MODIS_SP", "MODIS_NRT")}

def get(url):
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=180) as r:
                return r.read().decode()
        except Exception as e:
            print("   retry after error:", e)
            time.sleep(5 * (attempt + 1))
    sys.exit("Gave up on " + url.replace(KEY, "KEY"))

text = get(f"{BASE}/data_availability/csv/{KEY}/ALL")
if not text.startswith("data_id"):
    sys.exit("FIRMS said: " + text[:300])
(OUT / "data_availability.csv").write_text(text)
avail = {r["data_id"]: r for r in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text))}

for name, (sp, nrt) in SENSORS.items():
    sp_max = dt.date.fromisoformat(avail[sp]["max_date"])
    print(f"\n{name}  SP available to {sp_max}, NRT from {avail[nrt]['min_date']}")
    cols, rows, d = [], [], START
    while d <= END:
        src = sp if d <= sp_max else nrt
        last = min(d + dt.timedelta(days=4), END, sp_max if src == sp else END)
        n = (last - d).days + 1
        body = get(f"{BASE}/area/csv/{KEY}/{src}/{BBOX}/{n}/{d}")
        if body.strip() and not body.startswith("latitude"):
            sys.exit(f"FIRMS said on {d}: " + body[:300])
        got = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(body)))
        for r in got:
            r["source"] = src
            cols += [k for k in r if k not in cols]   # SP and NRT columns differ slightly
        rows += got
        print(f"  {d} to {last} {src:15s} {len(got):6d} rows")
        d = last + dt.timedelta(days=1)
        time.sleep(0.5)
    f = OUT / f"{name}_2026_kalimantan.csv"
    with open(f, "w", newline="") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=cols, restval="")
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"  saved {len(rows)} rows to {f.name}")







CautionTwo data versions in one year



SP data ends on 30 June, and the NRT data after it is provisional. NRT data also has no type flag, so fixed heat sources cannot be filtered out. A later check looks for them instead.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Study Design

Point Event Definition
A point event, or fire-day, is one 1 km cell with fire on one local day. Three facts about MODIS led to this.

MODIS sees each place up to four times a day, so one fire can be recorded four times.
Each detection is the centre of a pixel about 1 km wide, so distances under 1 km are not reliable.
FIRMS dates are in UTC. An Aqua night pass at 19:30 UTC is 02:30 the next day in Pulang Pisau (UTC+7).

So detections were converted to local time, placed on a 1 km grid and merged within each cell and day, keeping the most confident one.


Spatial Study Window
Pulang Pisau regency, using its GADM boundary, was chosen for three reasons.

It had the densest MODIS detections of any regency in Kalimantan in 2026 (Figure 2, Table 1).
At 9,740 km² it holds thousands of events but is small enough for the simulations to run in minutes.
Fire response and emergency status are decided at regency level.

The boundary cuts through peat, so fires just outside can affect fires inside. Edge corrections deal with this.


Temporal Study Window
Only one cleaned event fell before July, so the analysis covers 1 July to 22 September 2026 (84 days), with the day as the time unit.


Coordinate Reference System
All analysis uses UTM zone 49S (EPSG 32749). The eastern edge of the regency is just inside zone 50, but the distance error there is only about 0.13 percent, far smaller than a 1 km pixel. Distances are in kilometres.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Analytical Assumptions and Choices
The main choices are listed below and explained where they are used.



Decision
Choice
Why
Risk




Coordinates
UTM zone 49S, in km
Distances in km, same datum as FIRMS
Error of about 0.13 percent at the east edge


Event
One 1 km cell with fire on one local day
Merges repeat passes
One fire on a cell border can become two events


Time
Local day, UTC+7, 1 Jul to 22 Sep 2026
Matches daily fire management
Fires after 22 September are missed


KDE bandwidth
Scott, 7.5 km, plus 2 km and adaptive
Selectors under 1 km trace the pixel grid
Peak values change with bandwidth


STKDE bandwidths
Oversmoothing, 8.1 km and 2.6 days
Avoids false small hot spots
Short-lived hot spots are smoothed away


Distance range
1 to 15 km
Under 1 km is unreliable
Other distances are not tested


Edge correction
Border
Standard for large patterns
Loses points near the edge


Envelopes
Global, 99 simulations, nrank = 5
One 5 percent test for all distances
More cautious than pointwise envelopes


Q3 null model
Inhomogeneous Poisson from the KDE
Removes clustering caused by uneven density
Result changes with sigma, see Robustness Checks


Q4 null model
Dates shuffled, then shuffled within 10 km blocks
Keeps locations and each block’s timing
Block size is a judgement call


Q4 main test
Pairs under 3 km and 1 to 3 days apart
A range a patrol can cover
Chosen after seeing the grid


Q6 target
Cells with no fire in the past 7 days
What a patrol wants to find
Spread to the next cell counts as new

There are no missing coordinates, impossible values or duplicate rows. The real problems are the missing type flag in NRT data, repeat detections, UTC dates and low-confidence detections.


Deriving Local Time
ymd_hm() of lubridate builds a UTC timestamp from acq_date and acq_time. with_tz() moves it to Asia/Jakarta, which is UTC+7.



UTC to local time

modis <- modis_raw %>%
  mutate(t_utc      = ymd_hm(paste(acq_date, sprintf("%04d", acq_time)), tz = "UTC"),
         t_local    = with_tz(t_utc, "Asia/Jakarta"),
         date_local = as_date(t_local))

  count(satellite, daynight, name = "rows_shifted") %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Satellite", "Day (D) or night (N)", "Rows moved to the next day"),

6,026 detections change date, and every one is an Aqua night pass.






ImportantWhy the time fix matters



Without this fix, every Aqua night detection would be one day early. A space-time test would then see pairs of fires one day apart that were really on the same night.




Spatial and Confidence Filtering
st_as_sf() turns the table into points in WGS 84. st_transform() converts them to UTM 49S, and st_filter() keeps only the points inside Pulang Pisau.
FIRMS treats confidence under 30 as low, with more false alarms from sun glint or hot bare ground (Giglio et al., 2016). These detections are removed.



clip to Pulang Pisau and drop low confidence

modis_sf <- modis %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) %>%
  st_transform(32749)

pp_conf <- pp_det %>% filter(confidence >= 30)

All four daily passes see fires, even the one after midnight (730 detections), so one fire can be counted up to four times. This is why repeat detections are merged next. Cloud and smoke change between passes, so the counts do not show when fires burn.


Merging Repeated Detections
Each point gets a 1 km grid cell, and slice_max() keeps the most confident detection per cell and day.

xy <- st_coordinates(pp_conf)

  mutate(n_det = n()) %>%
  slice_max(confidence, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

The one-day drops, such as 16 and 17 September with 30 and 24 fire-days, are most likely cloud or smoke. The record also stops on 22 September with fires still burning, so the true peak may be later.

Burning Again in the Same Place

Many places burned more than once. Of the 3,065 fire-days, 1,503 were a cell burning for the first time. Another 46 percent were a cell that had burned in the past week, most often the day before (759 fire-days). For crews, this means a fire that looks finished may start again. For the analysis, a cell burning several days in a row creates space-time clustering by itself, so the Robustness Checks in Task 4 repeat the space-time test on newly burning cells only.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Kernel Density Estimation
KDE turns points into a smooth surface of fire-days per km². It is used instead of quadrat counts, which depend on where the grid is drawn. The bandwidth, sigma, sets how far each point is spread. A small sigma shows every small group of fires, and a large sigma blends them into wide zones.

Choosing the Bandwidth
spatstat’s bandwidth selectors give quite different answers.



four bandwidth selectors, in km

bw_tab <- tibble(
  selector = c("bw.diggle()", "bw.ppl()", "bw.scott.iso()", "bw.CvL()"),
  target   = c("Smallest error in the density estimate (Berman and Diggle)",
               "Best fit when each point is left out in turn",
               "Rule of thumb from how spread out the points are",
               "Density adds up correctly over the whole window"),
  sigma_km = c(bw.diggle(fire_ppp_u), bw.ppl(fire_ppp_u),
               bw.scott.iso(fire_ppp_u), bw.CvL(fire_ppp_u))
)
kable(bw_tab, digits = 2, col.names = c("Selector", "What it aims for", "Sigma (km)"))










Selector
What it aims for
Sigma (km)




bw.diggle()
Smallest error in the density estimate (Berman and Diggle)
0.64


bw.ppl()
Best fit when each point is left out in turn
0.84


bw.scott.iso()
Rule of thumb from how spread out the points are
7.53


bw.CvL()
Density adds up correctly over the whole window
9.53





bw.diggle() and bw.ppl() pick less than 1 km, smaller than a MODIS pixel, so they are ruled out. bw.scott.iso() gives 7.5 km and is the main bandwidth, and bw.CvL() gives 9.5 km. A 2 km surface is also shown, and the Robustness Checks repeat the tests at 5 km.
Assumptions. Every event counts equally, the smoothing is the same everywhere, and land just outside the boundary is like land inside.
adaptive.density() uses a narrower kernel where fires are dense and a wider one where they are sparse. It is the third map.



three density surfaces, events per km sq

kde_2   <- density(fire_ppp_u, sigma = 2, edge = TRUE, positive = TRUE)
kde_sc  <- density(fire_ppp_u, sigma = sig_scott, edge = TRUE, positive = TRUE)
kde_ad  <- adaptive.density(fire_ppp_u, method = "kernel")

to_rast <- function(im) {
  r <- rast(im)
  ext(r) <- as.vector(ext(r)) * 1000   # km back to metres
  crs(r) <- "EPSG:32749"
  r
}
kde_stack <- c(to_rast(kde_2), to_rast(kde_sc), to_rast(kde_ad))
names(kde_stack) <- c("Fixed, sigma 2 km",
                      paste0("Fixed, sigma ", round(sig_scott, 1), " km (Scott)"),
                      "Adaptive")



The PlotThe Code










Figure 8. Kernel density of fire-days, three bandwidth choices on one colour scale. Data from NASA FIRMS MODIS C6.1








tm_shape(kde_stack) +
  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "fixed",
              breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 16),
              labels = c("under 0.25", "0.25 to 0.5", "0.5 to 1", "1 to 2", "2 to 4", "4 or more"),
              values = "brewer.oranges"),

All three maps put the highest density in the south-central peat. The 2 km and adaptive maps also show smaller hot spots at the neck, on the east edge and in the north.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Spatio-Temporal Kernel Density
STKDE smooths over space and time together, so it avoids the fixed half-month breaks. spattemp.density() of sparr is used with oversmoothing bandwidths from OS.spattemp(), which are unlikely to create false small hot spots (Fernando and Hazelton, 2014; Davies, Marshall and Hazelton, 2018).
Assumptions. Space and time are smoothed separately, and sparr corrects for the start and end of the time window.



STKDE with oversmoothing bandwidths

bw_st <- OS.spattemp(fire_ppp_km)   # h in km, lambda in days

fire_stkde <- spattemp.density(fire_ppp_km, h = bw_st[1], lambda = bw_st[2])


Values are expected fire-days per 100 km² per day, so all six maps share one scale.

The PlotThe Code










Figure 9. Spatio-temporal kernel density on six days, expected fire-days per 100 km² per day. Data from NASA FIRMS MODIS C6.1

  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "fixed",
              breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 20),
              labels = c("under 0.5", "0.5 to 1", "1 to 2.5", "2.5 to 5", "5 to 10", "10 or more"),
              values = "brewer.oranges"),
            col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Fire-days per\n100 km² per day",
              position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
            col.free = FALSE) +
  tm_shape(pp_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey30") +
  tm_facets(ncol = 3) +
  tm_scalebar(position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom"), breaks = c(0, 20)) +
  tm_layout(panel.label.size = 1.1, panel.label.bg.color = "white") +
  tm_title("Burning moved from the narrow neck in July to the southern peat in September",
           size = 1.3, fontface = "bold")




In mid July and early August the main warm area is the neck. By 26 August the north and the south are warming, and by 18 September the south-central peat peaks at about 10 fire-days per 100 km² per day, with a second hot spot on the east edge.
The bandwidths are 8.1 km and 2.6 days, so short-lived hot spots are smoothed away. The neck burned weeks before the rest of the regency, which is worth checking in other years.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
How the Tests Work
Second-order analysis looks at pairs of events and asks whether they are closer together than a null model predicts. Each test names its null model.
The tests use Monte Carlo simulation. Many patterns are simulated from the null model, and their curves form a band called an envelope. An observed curve outside the envelope is a significant result. Global envelopes are used, which test all distances at once (Baddeley et al., 2015). With 99 simulations and nrank = 5, a pattern with no clustering would cross the envelope only 5 times in 100, so this is a test at the 5 percent level. Distances run from 1 to 15 km, since distances under 1 km are not reliable.
Border correction is used, which spatstat applies by default to large patterns. It only counts points far enough from the boundary, so distances stop at 15 km. Beyond that, almost no point in the narrow northern strip would still count.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: Q2. Are Fires More Clustered Than Random?
text:
Q2. Are Fires More Clustered Than Random?






NoteShort answer



Yes, strongly. The L function sits far above the random envelope, and the nearest fire is about half as far away as it would be at random (Clark-Evans ratio 0.48). Most of this comes from the uneven density already seen in Q1, so Q3 and Q4 dig further.




Question

Are fires closer together than they would be at random?

Method, and why

Besag’s L function, Lest(). L rescales Ripley’s K, which counts neighbours within distance r, so that L(r) − r is zero under randomness and a curve above the envelope means clustering. L is used instead of G or F because it uses all pairs, not only the nearest neighbour.

Compared with what

Complete spatial randomness (CSR). Every location is equally likely and fires are independent.

Assumptions

CSR assumes the same intensity everywhere. The first-order maps already show this is false, so this test is only a baseline.

Settings

1 to 15 km, border correction, 99-simulation global envelope with nrank = 5.






L function against CSR

set.seed(2026)
env_csr <- envelope(fire_ppp_u, Lest, nsim = 99, rmax = 15,
                    correction = "border", global = TRUE, nrank = 5, ginterval = c(1, 15),
                    savefuns = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)


The result is plotted in the left panel of Figure 10, under Q3. The observed curve is far above the envelope at every distance from 1 to 15 km.
The Clark-Evans ratio is 0.48, against about 1 under CSR, so the nearest fire is about half as far away as it would be at random. This is only a rough guide, because many nearest neighbours are under 1 km apart.
Repeat burning also adds to L. The 3,065 fire-days fall in only 1,503 cells, so a cell that burns on several days adds close pairs at every distance. This is another reason for the space-time test in Q4.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: Q3. Are Fires Still Clustered After Allowing for Density?
text:
Q3. Are Fires Still Clustered After Allowing for Density?






NoteShort answer



Not settled. Fires still cluster beyond a 7.5 km or 10 km density surface, but not beyond a 5 km one. One map cannot separate fires affecting each other from land that simply burns easily, so Q4 adds time.




Question

Do fires still cluster after allowing for uneven density?

Method, and why

The inhomogeneous L function, Linhom() (Baddeley, Møller and Waagepetersen, 2000). Pairs in dense areas count for less, so clustering that only comes from high density is removed.

Compared with what

An inhomogeneous Poisson process with the Scott KDE as its intensity. Fires are more likely where density is high but are still independent of each other.

Assumptions

The intensity surface must be right. If sigma is too small, the surface absorbs the clusters. If it is too large, uneven density shows up as clustering. One pattern cannot fully separate the two (Diggle, 2013).

Settings

Sigma 7.5 km with leave-one-out, so a fire does not count toward its own density. The intensity is estimated again for each simulation (Baddeley et al., 2015). The Robustness Checks try 5 and 10 km.






inhomogeneous L function against inhomogeneous Poisson

lam_sc <- density(fire_ppp_u, sigma = sig_scott, edge = TRUE, positive = TRUE)

set.seed(2026)
env_inhom <- envelope(fire_ppp_u, Linhom, nsim = 99, rmax = 15,
                      sigma = sig_scott, leaveoneout = TRUE,
                      simulate = expression(rpoispp(lam_sc)),
                      correction = "border", global = TRUE, nrank = 5, ginterval = c(1, 15),
                      savefuns = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)



The PlotThe Code










Figure 10. L(r) minus r with 99-simulation global envelopes and border correction, MODIS fire-days, Pulang Pisau








ggplot(env_df, aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = col_band, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = col_accent, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ test, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 15)) +
  labs(title = "Far more clustered than random, less so after allowing for density",
       subtitle = "Black is observed, dashed blue the null model average, orange the 95% envelope",
       x = "Distance r (km)", y = "L(r) minus r (km)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())




Reading the curves. Against CSR the observed curve is far above the envelope, at 5.8 km against an envelope top of 0.3 km at 5 km. Against the inhomogeneous null it is still above the envelope from 1.1 to 15 km, at 3.55 km against 0.88 km at 5 km.
The CSR result mostly confirms the KDE maps. The second result means fires have more neighbours than a 7.5 km density surface predicts, but with a 5 km bandwidth this disappears (see Robustness Checks). So the maps alone cannot show whether one fire raises the risk nearby. Q4 adds time to test this.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: Q4. Are Fires That Are Close in Space Also Close in Time?
text:
Q4. Are Fires That Are Close in Space Also Close in Time?






NoteShort answer



Yes. Fires under 3 km apart burned 1 to 3 days apart 1.33 times as often as chance, even with each 10 km block keeping its own fire season (p = 0.005). The result holds with VIIRS, for newly burning cells only, and for pairs 2 to 3 km apart.




Question

Are fires that are close in space also close in time, beyond each area’s own fire season?

Method, and why

A Knox-style test (Knox, 1964; Diggle et al., 1995). Pairs within 15 km are grouped by distance apart and days apart, and each group’s count is compared with 199 copies of the data with the dates shuffled among the fixed locations. STIKhat() from class is not used, because it assumes constant intensity unless one is supplied, and supplying one brings back the bandwidth problem.

Compared with, step 1

Dates shuffled across the whole regency. Locations and daily counts stay the same, so only the link between where and when is removed. This is not enough, because different areas burned at different times (Figure 9).

Compared with, step 2

Dates shuffled only within each 10 km block, so each block keeps its own fire season. Extra pairs left over come from fires closer than a block, either fires affecting each other or a fire front crossing a block.

Assumptions

Within a block, any date could have gone with any location. The 10 km block size is a judgement call.

Edge effects

No correction is needed, because locations never move. Pairs lost at the boundary are missing from the data and the shuffles alike.






Knox style space-time test, optional shuffling within blocks

knox_grid <- function(ppp, s_br, t_br, nsim = 199, rmax = 15, block = NULL) {
  n  <- npoints(ppp)
  tt <- marks(ppp)
  ds <- as.vector(dist(cbind(ppp$x, ppp$y)))
  ij <- which(lower.tri(matrix(0, n, n)), arr.ind = TRUE)   # same order as dist()
  keep <- ds <= rmax
  ds <- ds[keep]; i <- ij[keep, 1]; j <- ij[keep, 2]
  s_bin <- cut(ds, s_br, include.lowest = TRUE)
  tab <- function(tv) table(s_bin, cut(abs(tv[i] - tv[j]), t_br, include.lowest = TRUE))
  shuffle <- function() {
    if (is.null(block)) return(sample(tt))
    out <- tt
    for (b in unique(block)) {
      k <- which(block == b)
      out[k] <- tt[k][sample.int(length(k))]
    }
    out
  }
  obs  <- tab(tt)
  sims <- replicate(nsim, tab(shuffle()))
  list(obs = obs, sims = sims, expected = apply(sims, 1:2, mean),
       p = (1 + apply(sweep(sims, 1:2, obs, ">="), 1:2, sum)) / (nsim + 1))
}

# pooled test for the core, pairs under 3 km and 1 to 3 days apart
core_test <- function(k, rows = 1:3, cols = 2:3) {
  o <- sum(k$obs[rows, cols])
  s <- apply(k$sims[rows, cols, , drop = FALSE], 3, sum)
  tibble(ratio = round(o / mean(s), 2), p = (1 + sum(s >= o)) / (length(s) + 1))
}

s_breaks <- c(0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7.5, 10, 15)       # km
t_breaks <- c(-0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 3.5, 7.5, 14.5, 30.5, 90)   # days apart, same day kept on its own
block_10 <- paste(floor(fire_ppp_km$x / 10), floor(fire_ppp_km$y / 10))

set.seed(2026)
knox_free  <- knox_grid(fire_ppp_km, s_breaks, t_breaks)
set.seed(2026)
knox_block <- knox_grid(fire_ppp_km, s_breaks, t_breaks, block = block_10)

bind_rows(core_test(knox_free) %>% mutate(test = "Step 1, dates shuffled across the regency"),
          core_test(knox_block) %>% mutate(test = "Step 2, dates shuffled within 10 km blocks")) %>%
  select(test, ratio, p) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Null model", "Observed ÷ expected, under 3 km and 1 to 3 days", "p-value"))










Null model
Observed ÷ expected, under 3 km and 1 to 3 days
p-value




Step 1, dates shuffled across the regency
1.94
0.005


Step 2, dates shuffled within 10 km blocks
1.33
0.005





Same-day pairs are shown but not counted, since one large fire in a wide pixel can look like two. The main test pools pairs under 3 km and 1 to 3 days apart, a range a patrol can cover. These boxes were chosen after seeing the grid, so the Robustness Checks retest them on other data. The events fall into 85 blocks, and 7 blocks hold only one event.

The PlotThe Code










Figure 11. Observed over expected pairs of fire-days by distance and days apart, 199 shufflings for each step, MODIS, Pulang Pisau








ggplot(kx, aes(lag, dist, fill = pmin(pmax(log2(ratio), -2), 2))) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(sprintf("%.1f", ratio), sig)), size = 3.6) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = col_accent, mid = "white", high = col_fire, midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-2, 2), breaks = -2:2,
                       labels = c("1/4", "1/2", "1", "2", "4"),
                       name = "Observed /\nexpected") +
  geom_rect(data = tibble(test = sort(unique(kx$test))[2]), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            aes(xmin = 1.5, xmax = 3.5, ymin = 0.5, ymax = 3.5),
            fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ test) +
  labs(title = paste0("Pairs under 3 km and 1 to 3 days apart are ", core_test(knox_block)$ratio,
                      " times as common as with shuffled dates"),
       subtitle = "Black box, the main test. * marks boxes that beat 95% of 199 shufflings, uncorrected for 49 tests",
       x = "Days apart", y = "Distance apart (km)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        panel.grid = element_blank())




Fires close in space were also close in time. In step 1, pairs under 3 km and 1 to 3 days apart are 1.94 times as common as in the shuffles, mostly because different areas burned at different times. With each block’s timing fixed in step 2, they are still 1.33 times as common, about a third more (p = 0.005, the smallest possible).
The test cannot say whether fire spread, one person lit several plots, or fire moved through peat. With 708,650 pairs, small ratios can still be significant, and the extra pairs at 5 to 10 km and 31 to 90 days likely come from timing within blocks. Q6 in the Bonus section tests whether the result helps patrols.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Putting the Findings Together
The table below answers the integration questions from the brief, one per row.







Question
Answer from this study




What does first-order analysis show?
Fires were very uneven in space and time. Burning began at the neck in July, spread from late August and peaked in the south-central peat in September. Almost half of fire-days were a cell burning again within a week.


What does second-order analysis show?
Fires are far more clustered than random. After allowing for density, the answer depends on the bandwidth. The space-time test is clearer. Fires under 3 km apart were 1 to 3 days apart more often than random dates give.


How do they fit together?
The first-order maps show where to base crews. The space-time result, and the watch zone in the Bonus (Q6), show where to look each day.


Are the results consistent?
Mostly, as the next table shows. Only Q3 changes with the bandwidth.


Which assumptions matter most?
The density surface in Q3, and in Q4 the assumption that dates can be swapped within a 10 km block.


Other explanations?
Cloud hides fires on some days. One person lighting several plots looks the same as spread. A fire front crossing one block over a few days would also pass the Q4 test.



How consistent are the findings? Each finding below is checked against every analysis that bears on it.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Robustness Checks
Each check below changes one choice and reruns the tests.

Bandwidth in Q3. Sigma is set to 5 and 10 km as well as the Scott value.
Sensor. Everything is rerun on VIIRS, which has 375 m pixels and sees smaller fires. Its only data gap in the study period, 11 to 16 July, is before the main season.
Repeat burning. Q4 is rerun on newly burning cells only, which removes a cell burning day after day (Figure 5). Pairs 2 to 3 km apart are also tested alone, since one fire seen in two neighbouring cells is usually under 2 km apart.




check 1, inhomogeneous L at three bandwidths

linhom_check <- function(X, s, nsim = 99) {
  lam  <- density(X, sigma = s, edge = TRUE, positive = TRUE)
  sims <- rpoispp(lam, nsim = 2 * nsim)   # a global envelope needs a second set for the mean
  e <- envelope(X, Linhom, simulate = sims, nsim = nsim, rmax = 15,
                sigma = s, leaveoneout = TRUE, correction = "border",
                global = TRUE, nrank = 5, ginterval = c(1, 15), verbose = FALSE)
  d <- as.data.frame(e)
  tibble(sigma_km = round(s, 1),
         clustered = any(d$obs > d$hi),
         from_km = if (any(d$obs > d$hi)) round(min(d$r[d$obs > d$hi]), 1) else NA,
         to_km   = if (any(d$obs > d$hi)) round(max(d$r[d$obs > d$hi]), 1) else NA)
}

set.seed(2026)
sens_bw <- map_dfr(c(5, sig_scott, 10), ~ linhom_check(fire_ppp_u, .x))   # shown in the Q3 table below





check 2, rebuild events from VIIRS

viirs_raw <- read_csv("data/rawdata/firms/viirs_snpp_2026_kalimantan.csv")

viirs_ev <- viirs_raw %>%
  mutate(t_local    = with_tz(ymd_hm(paste(acq_date, sprintf("%04d", acq_time)), tz = "UTC"),
                              "Asia/Jakarta"),
         date_local = as_date(t_local)) %>%
  filter(confidence != "l",
         date_local >= as_date("2026-07-01"), date_local <= as_date("2026-09-22")) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(32749) %>%
  st_filter(pp_sf)

vxy <- st_coordinates(viirs_ev)
viirs_ev <- viirs_ev %>%
  mutate(cell = paste(floor(vxy[, 1] / 1000), floor(vxy[, 2] / 1000))) %>%
  group_by(cell, date_local) %>%
  slice_max(frp, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

viirs_ppp <- rescale.ppp(as.ppp(st_geometry(viirs_ev), W = pp_owin), 1000, "km")
marks(viirs_ppp) <- yday(viirs_ev$date_local)


VIIRS rows with low confidence (l) are removed, and the strongest detection is kept for each cell and day. This leaves 6,467 VIIRS events, about twice as many as MODIS.



check 2 and 3, rerun Q3 and Q4

sig_viirs <- as.numeric(bw.scott.iso(unmark(viirs_ppp)))
sens_viirs_l <- linhom_check(unmark(viirs_ppp), sig_viirs)

block_v <- paste(floor(viirs_ppp$x / 10), floor(viirs_ppp$y / 10))
set.seed(2026)
knox_viirs <- knox_grid(viirs_ppp, s_breaks, t_breaks, nsim = 99, block = block_v)

fires_new <- fires %>%
  arrange(cell, date_local) %>%
  group_by(cell) %>%
  mutate(gap_days = as.numeric(date_local - lag(date_local))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(is.na(gap_days) | gap_days > 7)

new_ppp <- rescale.ppp(as.ppp(st_geometry(fires_new), W = pp_owin), 1000, "km")
marks(new_ppp) <- fires_new$doy
block_n <- paste(floor(new_ppp$x / 10), floor(new_ppp$y / 10))

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: Q5. Do Roads and Canals Explain Where Fires Burn?
text:
Q5. Do Roads and Canals Explain Where Fires Burn?






NoteShort answer



Only partly. Fires burned within reach of roads and tracks, and just 4 of 3,065 fire-days were more than 14 km from one. But a model built on distance to roads, canals and rivers removes little of the clustering, so access is not the main reason fires group together.




Question

Are fires closer to roads and canals, and does this explain the clustering?

Why ask

Most peat fires are started by people (Page and Hooijer, 2016), who reach the peat by road and canal. Canals also dry the peat out.

Method

Distance maps are built from OSM. rhohat() shows how fire intensity changes with each distance. ppm() then fits a Poisson point process model, a kind of regression for points, using the three distances.

Compared with what

The fitted access model replaces the KDE as the null in an inhomogeneous L test, to see how much clustering is left once access is allowed for.




Preparing the OSM Layers
Only OSM features within 5 km of the regency are read, so fires near the boundary can still see canals just outside.



read OSM waterways and roads near Pulang Pisau

pp_buf  <- st_buffer(pp_sf, 5000)
bbox_wkt <- st_as_text(st_geometry(st_transform(pp_buf, 4326)))

waterways <- st_read("data/rawdata/osm/gis_osm_waterways_free_1.shp",
                     wkt_filter = bbox_wkt, quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(32749) %>% st_intersection(pp_buf)
roads <- st_read("data/rawdata/osm/gis_osm_roads_free_1.shp",
                 wkt_filter = bbox_wkt, quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(32749) %>% st_intersection(pp_buf)

bind_rows(waterways %>% mutate(layer = "waterways"), roads %>% mutate(layer = "roads")) %>%
  mutate(km = as.numeric(st_length(geometry)) / 1000) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(used_as = case_when(fclass %in% c("canal", "drain") ~ "Canal",
                             fclass == "river" ~ "River",
                             layer == "roads" & !fclass %in% c("footway", "steps", "pedestrian") ~ "Road or track",
                             TRUE ~ "Not used")) %>%
  group_by(used_as) %>%
  summarise(types = paste(unique(fclass[order(-km)])[1:min(4, n_distinct(fclass))], collapse = ", "),
            features = n(), km = round(sum(km)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(km)) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Used as", "Main OSM types", "Features", "Length (km)"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

Canals are OSM canals and drains. Roads include all roads, tracks and paths except footways. Rivers are a control, because deep peat domes form between rivers.



distance surfaces in km

to_psp <- function(x) {
  g <- st_geometry(st_cast(st_cast(x, "MULTILINESTRING"), "LINESTRING"))
  rescale.psp(as.psp(g, W = as.owin(pp_buf)), 1000, "km")
}
canal_psp <- to_psp(filter(waterways, fclass %in% c("canal", "drain")))
river_psp <- to_psp(filter(waterways, fclass == "river"))
road_psp  <- to_psp(filter(roads, !fclass %in% c("footway", "steps", "pedestrian")))

grid <- as.mask(pp_owin_km, dimyx = c(400, 200))
covs <- list(d_canal = distmap(canal_psp, xy = grid),
             d_road  = distmap(road_psp,  xy = grid),
             d_river = distmap(river_psp, xy = grid))




How Fire Intensity Changes with Distance

The PlotThe Code










Figure 12. Fire intensity as a function of distance, rhohat estimates with 95% bands. Each x axis stops at the 98th percentile of distances in the regency. Data from NASA FIRMS MODIS C6.1 and OpenStreetMap








rho_df <- imap_dfr(covs, function(im, nm) {
  d <- as.data.frame(rhohat(fire_ppp_u, im)) %>% rename(X = 1)
  cap <- quantile(im[pp_owin_km, drop = TRUE], 0.98, na.rm = TRUE)
  d %>% filter(X <= cap) %>% mutate(covariate = nm)
}) %>%
  mutate(covariate = recode(covariate, d_canal = "Distance to canal or drain",
                            d_road = "Distance to road or track",
                            d_river = "Distance to river"),
         covariate = factor(covariate, levels = c("Distance to road or track",
                            "Distance to canal or drain", "Distance to river")))
avg_int <- intensity(fire_ppp_u)

ggplot(rho_df, aes(X, rho)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = col_band, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(colour = col_fire, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = avg_int, colour = col_accent, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ covariate, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Almost no fire burned more than 14 km from a road or track",
       subtitle = "Dashed blue line is the regency-wide average intensity",
       x = "Distance (km)", y = "Fire-days per km²") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())




Almost all fires were within reach of a road or track. Intensity stays near or above average up to about 12 km from one, then drops to almost zero. Only 4 of 3,065 fire-days were more than 14 km away, although that land is 16 percent of the regency. 82 percent of fire-days were within 5 km of a road or canal, against 65 percent of the land.
Intensity rises far from rivers, which fits peat domes. The canal curve is noisy, with peaks 50 to 60 km from any mapped canal in the northern strip, where OSM shows almost no canals. The curves show where fires burned, not why.


Fitting the Access Model



Poisson point process models with OSM covariates

m_null   <- ppm(fire_ppp_u ~ 1)
m_access <- ppm(fire_ppp_u ~ log(d_canal + 0.5) + log(d_road + 0.5) + log(d_river + 0.5),
                data = covs)

         meaning = c("", "Fewer fires further from canals", "Fewer fires further from roads",

sims_access <- rpoispp(predict(m_access), nsim = 198)
env_access <- envelope(fire_ppp_u, Linhom, simulate = sims_access, nsim = 99,

                       global = TRUE, nrank = 5, ginterval = c(1, 15), verbose = FALSE)
